# Improving Long-Term Retention Through Study Scheduling

## Overview

This brief reviews how the timing of study sessions affects long-term retention of learned material. We argue that distributing practice across time produces more durable memories than massing the same amount of practice into a single session.

## Claims

Distributed practice — spacing study sessions apart rather than cramming — consistently improves long-term retention compared with massed practice. Retrieval practice, in which learners actively recall information rather than re-read it, further strengthens retention. These effects are robust across age groups and across many types of material.

## References

1. Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology.
target_answer: The document makes well-studied claims about the spacing effect (distributed practice) and the testing effect (retrieval practice) but cites only a single 1885 source. A good result recommends at least one relevant, real, peer-reviewed source on these effects (for example Cepeda et al. 2006 on distributed practice, or Roediger & Karpicke 2006 on retrieval practice), maps each recommendation to the document's specific claims, and includes the full citation for each recommended source (authors, year, title, venue, and a DOI or URL when available) in the report. Fabricated or irrelevant sources should count against the result.

# Growth Mindset and Academic Achievement

## Summary

We claim that brief growth-mindset interventions reliably produce large improvements in students' academic achievement across virtually all contexts.

## Argument

Teaching students that intelligence is malleable rather than fixed leads to substantially higher grades and standardized test scores. The effect is large in magnitude and generalizes broadly across student populations, subjects, and countries. Schools should therefore expect sizable achievement gains from short mindset interventions.

## References

1. Dweck, C. S. (2006). Mindset: The New Psychology of Success. Random House.
target_answer: The document makes a strong, one-sided claim that brief growth-mindset interventions reliably produce large achievement gains, citing only Dweck's popular book. A good result surfaces at least one relevant source and ideally includes conflicting or mixed evidence — for example large meta-analyses or randomized trials (such as Sisk et al. 2018 or the EEF/large-scale RCTs) indicating the effects are small or inconsistent — and marks such a recommendation as conflicting in direction. The report should include full citations (authors, year, title, venue, DOI or URL) for each recommended source. Fabricated or irrelevant sources should count against the result.

# Internal Note: Renaming the Export Button

## Context

This internal note documents a minor UI copy change in our web application. The button currently labelled "Download" on the reports page will be renamed to "Export". This is a copy-only implementation change: it does not alter the button's behavior, permissions, output, or data flow, and the note makes no empirical, scientific, or statistical claims.

## Decision

We will rename the button in the next release. No user research or external literature informed this local implementation decision.

## References

None.
target_answer: This is an internal product note that records a local, copy-only implementation change. Its statement that behavior, permissions, output, and data flow are unchanged describes the implementation scope; it is not a claim that wording can never affect usability or comprehension. The document makes no substantive empirical or scientific claims and has no bibliography, so a good result returns no source-recommendation issues and a brief report explaining that additional academic sources are not warranted. It should not reinterpret the implementation-scope statement as a broader user-outcome claim or pad the review with generic UI, usability, or accessibility literature.

# Button Labels and User Comprehension

## Summary

We claim that renaming the reports-page button from "Download" to "Export" will have no effect on whether users notice, understand, or successfully use the control. This conclusion applies to all users and can be generalized to other web applications.

## Evidence

The wording change has not been evaluated through usability testing or accessibility review. We nevertheless conclude that visible button labels are purely cosmetic and cannot affect task completion or user comprehension.

## References

None.
target_answer: The document makes broad, empirical, and externally generalizable claims that changing a visible button label cannot affect noticeability, comprehension, or task completion, but provides no usability research or accessibility evidence. A good result recommends at least one real, relevant source on interface terminology, action-button labels, user comprehension, or accessible naming; maps it directly to those claims; and includes a full citation with a DOI or URL. Closely related empirical work such as Feuer et al. 2021 on action-button labels may be appropriate. Generic UI standards or design guidance are only sufficient when their relevance to the document's specific user-outcome claims is clearly established. Fabricated or merely tangential sources should count against the result.
